prompt.context: Our client is a major pest control company operating in the US South East. The client sells extermination services for the home and garden. The client is looking to improve their profitability, and is asking for specific recommendations to effect this. They do not have a target profit margin, but they are interested in exploring the full range of options presented to them.
prompt.question: What areas should we consider to improve the client's profitability? Provide specific recommendations.

clarifying_info.q: What services does the client offer?
clarifying_info.a: They sell extermination services for the home and garden, including one-time fumigations and routine sprayings.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a target profit margin?
clarifying_info.a: No specific target; the client is interested in exploring the full range of options.
Customer growth is currently 0% — the client is neither gaining nor losing clients — even though the broader market is growing at a healthy rate.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client acquire customers?
clarifying_info.a: Through a call center, which covers all customer interactions.

exhibits.title: Call Center Effectiveness and Customer Turnover
exhibits.shows: Left side: data on how effective the client is at converting prospective callers into customers (call volume and yield rate). Right side: annual turnover rate of the existing customer base and total account count.

framework: Revenues: pricing (one-time vs. recurring services), customer acquisition (call conversion), customer retention (churn/attrition)
Costs: labor (call center staff, field technicians), materials/chemicals, territory coverage efficiency, overhead
Customer acquisition funnel: call volume, yield rate, onboarding process
Customer retention: contract terms, service quality, competitive alternatives
Pricing strategy: price per service type, average revenue per account
Operational efficiency: route density, scheduling, technician productivity

questions.prompt: What aspects of revenue are important for a pest control company?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify Price x Quantity framework applied specifically to pest control: (1) pricing for different service types (one-time fumigation vs. routine/recurring sprayings) and (2) customer acquisition and retention driving the volume of accounts.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm the factors that would play into a customer's decision of whether or not to buy the client's services.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure their brainstorm. Strong answers include: (1) Need/urgency — severity of infestation, seasonal factors, geographic pest prevalence; (2) Price sensitivity — cost of service vs. DIY alternatives, income level; (3) Trust/brand — reputation, reviews, licensing, guarantees; (4) Convenience — scheduling ease, speed of response, online booking; (5) Awareness — marketing reach, word-of-mouth, referrals; (6) Competitive alternatives — other providers, hardware store products.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, how many clients are gained and lost each year? Do the numbers reconcile with the stated 0% net growth?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute new customers from the call center and lost customers from annual turnover, then confirm net = 0.

math.setup: Annual calls = 4,200 * 12 = 50,400 ≈ 50,000 (round). New customers = 50,000 * 20% yield = 10,000. Lost customers = 500,000 accounts * 2% turnover = 10,000. Net = 10,000 - 10,000 = 0.
steps: 500,000 accounts * 2% annual turnover = 10,000 customers lost per year
math.answer: 10,000 customers gained, 10,000 customers lost; net growth = 0.

questions.prompt: What is the average price the client charges for its services?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize they need revenue and total accounts, then compute average price per account.

math.setup: Average price = Total Revenue / Total Accounts
math.answer: $100 average price per account per year

questions.prompt: Given the data, which levers — pricing, attrition, or call yield — offer the most opportunity for improvement?
questions.guidance: Strong candidate reasoning: (1) Pricing is difficult to raise in a competitive commodity-like service industry without risking churn; (2) 2% annual attrition is already quite low — hard to meaningfully reduce further; (3) Improving call yield from 20% offers the clearest lever for growth, since the market is growing and inbound call volume could increase.

questions.prompt: The call center staff is split into three equal thirds: 30% yield, 20% yield, and 10% yield. What do you recommend to improve overall yield?
questions.guidance: Candidate should suggest: (1) Identify and turn over the bottom-third (10% yield) employees — the case notes it is apparent within the first week which bucket a new hire falls into; (2) Have top-third (30% yield) employees coach new hires and share best practices; (3) Implement structured training programs based on top performers' techniques; (4) Revise hiring criteria and screening based on attributes of high-yield staff.

math.setup: Current blended yield = (30% + 20% + 10%) / 3 = 20%. If bottom third is replaced and all staff achieve at least 20% yield (or top-third average), blended yield improves.
steps: If bottom third is removed and replaced with 20%-yield staff: 1/3*30% + 1/3*20% + 1/3*20% = 10%+6.7%+6.7% = 23.3%
If all staff achieve top-third standard (30%): yield = 30%, new customers = 50,000*30% = 15,000 vs. current 10,000
math.answer: Replacing bottom-third with average-yield staff raises blended yield from 20% to ~23%. Coaching to top-third standard could raise it to 30%, adding 5,000 net new customers per year.

brainstorming.prompt: How could the client improve the yield of its call center (converting prospective callers into paying customers)?

categories.name: Training & Coaching
ideas: Have top-performing (30% yield) staff coach new hires
Develop scripts or talk-tracks based on top performers
Record and review calls for quality feedback

categories.name: Hiring & Staffing
ideas: Improve screening to identify high-yield candidates
Use probationary first week to assess yield potential and act quickly
Increase staff size to reduce wait times and abandoned calls

categories.name: Technology & Process
ideas: CRM to track caller history and personalize follow-up
Automated callback or follow-up for interested but unconverted callers
Improve call routing to direct leads to high-yield agents
Reduce hold times to prevent drop-off

categories.name: Pricing & Offer
ideas: Introductory discount or free first inspection to reduce friction
Flexible scheduling options mentioned during call
Bundled packages (one-time + routine) offered on the call

recommendation: The primary opportunity is improving call center yield from the current 20% blended average
Implement a training program where top-third (30% yield) staff coach new hires and share best practices
Turn over the bottom-third (10% yield) staff, replacing them with better-screened candidates — identifiable within the first week
These actions directly address the stagnant customer growth in an expanding market without requiring difficult price increases or major attrition reduction efforts
risks: Turnover of bottom-third staff increases short-term recruiting and onboarding costs
Training program requires time investment from top performers, potentially reducing their own call volume temporarily
Market growth may slow, reducing the pool of inbound callers regardless of yield improvement
next_steps: Analyze attributes of top-performing staff to improve hiring criteria
Design and pilot a structured coaching program led by top-third agents
Set yield improvement targets (e.g., raise blended yield to 25%+) and track weekly
Assess whether call volume can be grown through marketing to take full advantage of yield improvement
